clue.text: Comeback for old black Sunday hats

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the letters built from the following words are read from the end back to the start

blocks.note: swart is an archaic word for black or swarthy
S is the standard abbreviation for Sunday

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned black Sunday hats making a return to fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: SWART plus S, read backwards, gives STRAWS; a straw is a straw hat such as a boater.
explanation.definitionFit: Straws, short for straw hats like boaters and panamas, are headwear woven from dried stalks.

blocks.note: first meaning: a drop of water from the eye when crying
second meaning, a verb: to rush along at great pace

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently, which helps hide them: one rhymes with 'ear', the other with 'air'.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the salty droplet shed while weeping; the other is to rush along recklessly, as in tearing down a road.

blocks.note: surface reading: a riding habit, the outfit worn by a rider in the saddle
setter's reading: horse is slang for heroin, so someone on horse is a drug user, whose habit is a dependency

explanation.surface: A question about what clothing a rider should wear.
explanation.walkthrough: Habit looks like riding clothes; here it is a compulsive dependency, and horse is street slang for heroin.
explanation.definitionFit: An addiction is a compulsive dependence on a drug, which users commonly call their habit.

indicators.note: without a heart means the middle of the following phrase is cut away, keeping only its ends

blocks.note: the whole phrase taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A guard who has been ostracised without any sympathy.
explanation.walkthrough: To send someone to Coventry is a British idiom for refusing to speak to them. Remove the central TOCOVENT and SENT plus RY remain: SENTRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentry is a soldier posted to keep watch at a gate or camp, which is what a guard does.

blocks.note: Walt Disney, the animation pioneer
animation in the sense of liveliness or zest

explanation.surface: A quoted title, apparently a Disney cartoon set in the Land of Oz.
explanation.walkthrough: The source text has lost the opening quote and W, so the definition reads 'Walking in Oz'. Oz is Australia, where to go waltzing Matilda is to tramp the roads with a swag.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian slang to waltz is to travel on foot carrying one's bundle, as in the song Waltzing Matilda.

blocks.note: first meaning: a jokey description of a plump person
second meaning, literally: a sofa or chair generously padded

explanation.walkthrough: The literal sense describes furniture; applied to people it is a humorous euphemism for being overweight.
explanation.definitionFit: A well-padded armchair is generously covered and filled; the same phrase is a polite joke for a plump, rounded person.

blocks.note: peers of the realm
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: Aristocrats who share power between them.
explanation.walkthrough: Joint authority looks like a single phrase about shared power; joint is a body part and authority stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Lordship means dominion or rule over territory or people, a form of power and command.

blocks.note: surface reading: Peter Shaffer's play Equus staged or filmed in monochrome
setter's reading: Equus is the horse genus, and its striped African member is coloured black and white

explanation.surface: A production of the play Equus shot in black and white.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks suggest the stage play; Equus is also the Latin name of the horse genus, which includes the striped species.
explanation.definitionFit: The zebra is an African wild horse of genus Equus with a coat of bold black and white stripes.

blocks.note: surface reading: something that silences scruffy, untidy people
setter's reading: the scruff is the back of the neck, and things that muffle it are wrapped round it

explanation.surface: Something that keeps shabby ruffians quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: Scruffs looks like scruffy people and muffle like silencing; here muffle means wrap up warmly and the scruff is the nape.
explanation.definitionFit: Neckcloths are cravats or scarves wound round the throat and nape, keeping that area wrapped and warm.

blocks.note: first meaning: a bright scarlet colour, also the robe colour of senior Catholic clergy
second meaning: one is a counting number as opposed to first, an ordinal

explanation.walkthrough: 'A red one' reads as a single phrase about a red thing; split it after 'red'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardinal is a deep scarlet shade, and cardinal numbers such as one, two and three express quantity.

indicators.note: something used is worked over and knocked about, so the name before it is rearranged

blocks.note: the tennis player's surname taken as letters

explanation.surface: Tennis star Boris Becker played with a strung racket.
explanation.walkthrough: Something with strings suggests Becker's racket; it is a medieval bowed instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The rebeck is a medieval fiddle, a bowed instrument with usually three strings.

blocks.note: first meaning: formal display and ritual
second meaning: the word paired with Pomp in the title of Elgar's marches

explanation.walkthrough: Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance marches take their title from Othello, where circumstance means ceremonial formality.
explanation.definitionFit: Circumstance in an old sense means formal ceremonial display, and it follows Pomp in the title of Elgar's famous marches.

blocks.note: first meaning: perfectly clean, without a mark
second meaning: flawless, exactly right

explanation.walkthrough: The play is on spot: one meaning has none, the other is precisely correct.
explanation.definitionFit: Immaculate describes both a perfectly clean, unblemished surface and a faultless, precise performance.

clue.text: Ahab's father brought in kingdom rituals

indicators.note: brought in means held inside, so the letters sit within the next two words

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A biblical king introducing royal ceremonies to his realm.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Bible Omri was a king of Israel and father of King Ahab, so this is general knowledge, not Moby-Dick's captain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Books of Kings name Omri, ruler of the northern Israelite realm, as the parent of King Ahab.

clue.text: Hole 13 made up part of the Wentworth inheritance, say

definitions.text: part of the Wentworth inheritance, say

indicators.note: made up means invented or put together anew, so the letters are assembled in fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
the answer to 13 across

explanation.surface: A golf hole at Wentworth, the famous Surrey course, forming part of a family estate.
explanation.walkthrough: Hole and Wentworth suggest golf; Wentworth is also the name of great English houses whose contents pass down the generations.
explanation.definitionFit: An heirloom is a valued object handed down through a family, so it forms part of what heirs receive; 'say' marks Wentworth as an example.

clue.text: Chile leek cooked in the old doctor's manner

indicators.note: ingredients that are cooked are transformed, so the vegetables' letters are reworked

blocks.note: the two words taken as letters

explanation.surface: A recipe for a leek dish from Chile prepared the traditional way.
explanation.walkthrough: Leech is an archaic word for a physician, from the bloodsucking worms doctors once applied.
explanation.definitionFit: Leech was an old word for physician, so behaving like one means acting as a medieval physician would.

blocks.note: plain in the sense of flat or level
a chant is a sung melody

explanation.surface: A church service with plainsong sung by the choir.
explanation.walkthrough: Plainchant looks like one word for church music; split it into plain and chant.
explanation.definitionFit: Evensong is the Anglican evening prayer service, often sung by a choir in cathedrals.

clue.text: Rival can upset this festive occasion

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the preceding letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the two words taken as letters

explanation.surface: A competitor might spoil the celebrations.
explanation.definitionFit: A carnival is a public celebration with parades and revelry, a festival held before Lent.

indicators.note: without a heart, the girl's name loses its central letter
teased hair or fibres are pulled apart and loosened, so the remaining letters are disordered

blocks.note: the name taken as letters

explanation.surface: A cruel Chloe mocked a woodland spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the middle L leaves CHOE, which is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Echo was a mountain spirit who pined for Narcissus until only her voice remained.

blocks.note: first meaning: evaded, parried a question as a swordsman parries a thrust
second meaning: enclosed with a boundary round its border

explanation.walkthrough: The rhyming pair looks like one idea; each is a separate sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Fenced means both evasively parried, as when dodging questions, and enclosed by a barrier along a boundary.

clue.text: Saw property that could make a baby cry

definitions.text: Saw property that could make a baby cry

blocks.note: setter's reading: a feature of the carpentry tool, whose serrated edge slices wood

blocks.clueFragment: that could make a baby cry
blocks.note: surface reading: the painful process when an infant's first molars come through the gums

explanation.surface: Something about a saw that might upset an infant.
explanation.walkthrough: Saw looks like the past tense of see; it is the tool, and the phrase also names an infant's teething.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw's serrated blade has sharp points that slice wood, and an infant whose first teeth emerge suffers painful gums.

clue.text: Old Algerian soldier serving a foreign court

indicators.note: something foreign is strange and outlandish, so the next word's letters come out in an unfamiliar order

blocks.note: taken as letters

explanation.surface: A veteran North African soldier serving at a royal court abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Serving a foreign court reads as a soldier's posting; foreign is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Turcos were Algerian light infantrymen in the nineteenth-century French army, now a historical term.

indicators.note: the phrase says a word is heard rather than read, so the spoken form of the next word counts

blocks.note: top in the sense of summit

explanation.surface: Something resembles the leading dog of the pack.
explanation.walkthrough: Top dog reads as one phrase; peke is short for Pekingese.
explanation.definitionFit: A peke is a Pekingese, a small long-haired toy breed originally kept by Chinese emperors.

indicators.note: ordered means put into a new arrangement, so the preceding words' letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the three words taken as letters

explanation.surface: Someone at the barber's recalls a trim they got or requested.
explanation.walkthrough: Ordered seems to mean requested from the barber; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut is a haircut, the style a hairdresser gives, which is what a hairdo is.

blocks.note: first meaning: a fence, one who handles stolen goods
second meaning: a satellite dish that picks up broadcast signals

explanation.walkthrough: 'A criminal dish' reads as a wicked meal; split it after 'criminal'.
explanation.definitionFit: A receiver is someone who knowingly accepts stolen goods, and also an aerial apparatus that picks up broadcast signals.

clue.text: Attached to gold and been corrupted

indicators.note: something corrupted is spoiled and degraded, so the preceding letters come out scrambled

blocks.note: taken as letters
taken as letters

explanation.surface: Someone so devoted to riches that wealth has spoiled them.
explanation.walkthrough: Gold and been looks like a grammatical slip; together they are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Belonged, as in belonged to a club, means was a member of or was connected with something.

blocks.note: first meaning: a person who gives up certain foods
second meaning: one who practises Banting, the Victorian low-carbohydrate regime named after William Banting

explanation.walkthrough: Banter looks like teasing talk; here it is a bant-er, a follower of William Banting's nineteenth-century slimming regime.
explanation.definitionFit: A dieter restricts what they eat to slim, as followers of Banting's regime did by giving up starch and sugar.
